question_text:
A 16-year-old Caucasian boy presents to your family practice office complaining of itchiness. He denies other symptoms. He also denies tobacco, alcohol, or other illicit drug use and is not sexually active. He has no other significant past medical or surgical history aside from a meniscal repair from a wrestling injury sustained two years ago from which he has recovered fully. Vitals are T 98.3, HR 67, BP 110/70. On exam you note several pruritic, erythematous, slightly raised annular patches with central clearing on his back.

Which of the following additional tests or features are sufficient to make the diagnosis of this boy's skin lesion?

                    ### Question
                    A 16-year-old Caucasian boy presents to your family practice office complaining of itchiness. He denies other symptoms. He also denies tobacco, alcohol, or other illicit drug use and is not sexually active. He has no other significant past medical or surgical history aside from a meniscal repair from a wrestling injury sustained two years ago from which he has recovered fully. Vitals are T 98.3, HR 67, BP 110/70. On exam you note several pruritic, erythematous, slightly raised annular patches with central clearing on his back.

Which of the following additional tests or features are sufficient to make the diagnosis of this boy's skin lesion?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Acid-fast bacilli on smear from skin scrapings
opb. History of recent herald patch and lesions along skin cleavage lines
opc. Presence of hyphae when KOH added to skin scrapings
opd. Symmetrical distribution on bilaterial extremities progressing proximally
ope. History of time spent in a Lyme-endemic region

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient's presentation of pruritic, erythematous, annular patches with central clearing is highly suggestive of tinea corporis, a fungal infection. The most definitive test for this diagnosis is the presence of hyphae when KOH is added to skin scrapings, confirming the diagnosis of tinea. The alternative diagnosis of pityriasis rosea could be considered if there was a history of a herald patch, but this is less likely without that history. Granuloma annulare typically presents with symmetrical distribution, but this is not a definitive diagnostic criterion. Lyme disease requires a history of exposure to endemic areas and specific serological testing for confirmation, which is not indicated here. Cutaneous tuberculosis is rare and would require acid-fast bacilli on smear, which is not a common finding in this context. Therefore, the most relevant and sufficient test to confirm the diagnosis is the presence of hyphae in KOH preparations.
